query: For Q235 steel in its pre-exposure state, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the onset or suppression of corrosion-related degradation in harsh environments at room and elevated temperatures? Specify a controlled study that would isolate the governing cause, predicted observations relative to the untreated reference, applicable boundary conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive falsification result.

generation.hypothesis: Enhancing the formation of a thin, thermally reinforced iron oxide layer on the surface of pre-exposed Q235 steel can suppress its corrosion degradation in harsh environments.
generation.material_initial_state: Q235 steel in its untreated, as-received pre-exposure state with its native microstructure and existing surface heterogeneities.
generation.intervention: A controlled thermal treatment designed to accelerate and stabilize the formation of a protective iron oxide (primarily Fe2O3) film on the steel surface prior to exposure in harsh environments.
generation.conditions: Testing in standardized aggressive environments (for example, saline or acidified aqueous solutions) at room temperature (≈25 °C) and at an elevated temperature (e.g., 150–200 °C), with well-controlled humidity and exposure durations.
generation.structural_mediator: The development of a continuous and adherent passive iron oxide layer that reduces the active metal exposed to the corrosive medium.
generation.mechanism: Thermal treatment enhances oxidation kinetics such that a uniform, slightly thickened iron oxide layer forms that is mechanically robust and chemically inert; at elevated temperatures, the kinetics further favor stabilization of the oxide film, slowing the corrosion reaction rate by reducing the available metal surface area for anodic dissolution.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated Q235 steel, thermally pre-treated steel will exhibit reduced corrosion rates, as indicated by lower mass loss, fewer localized corrosion sites (pitting), and a more uniform oxide morphology on SEM and XPS characterization. These differences are expected to be pronounced at elevated temperatures where the formation kinetics and stability of the passivating film are enhanced.
generation.baseline: Corrosion behavior of untreated Q235 steel exposed to the same harsh chemical environments at room and elevated temperatures.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is applicable only for Q235 steel in its as-received state and under environmental conditions that are sufficiently aggressive to initiate corrosion yet allow for passivation (e.g., the presence of moderate chloride concentrations and controlled temperature ranges up to around 200 °C). Extremely high temperatures or corrosive media that destroy the oxide layer completely fall outside the predicted domain.
generation.uncertainty: While strong theoretical support exists from general passivation behavior in steels, direct quantitative data on the optimal thermal treatment parameters and the exact correlation between oxide film characteristics and corrosion suppression in Q235 under these specific conditions are limited. The magnitude of improvement in corrosion resistance is therefore uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two groups of Q235 steel samples: one set receives the controlled thermal treatment to promote oxide layer formation, while the control group remains untreated. Expose both groups to identical harsh aqueous environments (e.g., controlled saline solution exposures) at room and elevated temperatures for a fixed period. Monitor the evolution of surface oxide layers using SEM and XPS, and measure corrosion rates via weight loss and electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS).
measurements: Surface morphology and oxide film thickness (by SEM)
Chemical composition of the film (by XPS)
Corrosion rate by weight loss analysis
Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy (EIS) to assess protective film performance
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If thermally pre-treated samples exhibit corrosion rates (mass loss, pitting density, and lower impedance values) that are statistically indistinguishable from or greater than those of untreated samples under both room and elevated temperature conditions, then the hypothesis that the thermally reinforced oxide layer suppresses corrosion is falsified.
